body.en:
• Compile-time errors: caught by javac - syntax slips, type mismatches, missing semicolons. No .class file is produced until they are fixed.
  • Runtime errors (exceptions): the program compiles cleanly but blows up while running - divide by zero, null reference, array index out of range. The JVM throws an exception object describing what went wrong and where.
  • Logical errors: the program compiles and runs, yet the answer is wrong - a formula slip, an inverted condition. No compiler or JVM ever warns you; only testing does.

Run jv4_1 to see all three side by side, then jv4_2 to watch an unhandled runtime error kill a program mid-way.

• Every throwable object descends from Throwable, which splits into Error (serious JVM problems - not meant to be caught) and Exception (application problems - designed to be caught).
  • Under Exception sits RuntimeException - the unchecked family. javac never forces you to handle these: ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, NumberFormatException, IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException.
  • Other Exception children are checked: javac requires either try-catch or a throws clause - e.g. InterruptedException, IOException.
  • Why it matters: knowing an exception's family tells you whether the compiler will help you remember to handle it.

• try { ... } wraps the risky statements; catch (SomeException e) { ... } holds the recovery plan.
  • The moment a statement inside try throws, control jumps to the matching catch - the rest of the try block is skipped for that run.
  • e is the exception object: e.getMessage() gives the detail string, e.getClass().getSimpleName() gives the exact type.
  • After the catch completes, execution resumes AFTER the whole try-catch - the program survives.

Practical 13 walkthrough: jv4_3 and jv4_4 catch the two required built-ins - divide by zero and null pointer.

• finally { ... } attaches to a try (with or without catch) and runs on every path: normal completion, caught exception, even uncaught exception (right before the crash).
  • That one guarantee makes finally the home of cleanup: closing files and connections, releasing locks, printing audit logs.
  • Order of blocks is fixed: try, then catch(es), then finally. Only one catch ever runs, but finally ALWAYS runs.

jv4_7 calls bank() twice - success and failure - and "close vault" prints both times. That is finally keeping its promise.

• One try may own several catch clauses; the JVM tests them top to bottom and runs the first whose type matches the thrown object (matching is by IS-A - a parent type matches child objects).
  • Because of IS-A matching, order must run specific first, general last. A parent catch placed higher swallows everything below.
  • javac enforces this: a catch unreachable because of an earlier parent catch is a compile error.

jv4_6 parses a too-big number and the NumberFormatException catch wins; jv4_11 shows the NPE catch beating its RuntimeException parent written below it.

• throw new ExceptionType("message") creates and raises an exception object on the spot - a single object, so the word is singular.
  • The remainder of the method is skipped; the JVM hunts for a matching catch up the call chain.
  • Main use: validation - reject impossible data (negative age, overdrawn balance) the moment it appears, with a message the catch can show to a human.
  • Any class from the hierarchy may be thrown; RuntimeException children keep it unchecked.

jv4_8 refuses under-18 voters with IllegalArgumentException - a built-in type used by our own logic.

h.en: throws: Declaring Risk in the Header

body.en:
• A method that might raise a checked exception must say so: void f() throws InterruptedException { ... }.
  • This is a warning, not an action - it pushes the duty onto the caller, who must catch the exception or declare throws again.
  • Several types can be listed with commas: throws IOException, InterruptedException.
  • throw vs throws: throw is a statement that raises one object inside the body; throws is a clause in the signature that advertises what may come out. jv4_9 and jv4_10 contrast the two.

h.en: Need of Collections and the Hierarchy

body.en:
• Arrays are fixed-size and type-naked; real programs need containers that grow, search, and remove - that is the Collections framework (package java.util).
  • Top of the family: interface Collection; below it interfaces List and Set; concrete classes such as ArrayList and HashSet implement them.
  • Collections store objects, not primitives - autoboxing (Unit 2) wraps int into Integer automatically when you add.
  • Design habit: declare with the interface type (List<String> l = new ArrayList<>();) and construct with the class - swapping implementations later costs one word.

• ArrayList<E> - the growable array: add(e) appends, add(i, e) inserts, get(i)/set(i, e) access by index, size() replaces array length.
  • Remove by value remove("Farhan") or by index remove(0); the list shrinks and re-indexes itself.
  • Search: contains(e) answers yes/no, indexOf(e) answers where (-1 when absent).
  • Printing the list object itself shows [a, b, c] - friendly toString included.

Practical 14 walkthrough: jv4_12 performs add, remove and search exactly as the practical demands.

• The enhanced for loop - for (String t : team) { ... } - visits every element left to right with no index bookkeeping.
  • Works on any List or Set (any Collection), so one syntax covers the whole framework.
  • Limits: no index inside the body, and you cannot add/remove elements of the collection while iterating (that throws ConcurrentModificationException in real programs).
  • Keep the classic counting loop for tasks that genuinely need positions.

jv4_13 runs both loops on the same ArrayList of marks and totals them with for-each.

• HashSet<E> stores each element once: re-adding an equal value is silently ignored - perfect for unique tags, roll numbers, friend lists.
  • contains() is a hash-table lookup - near-instant even for huge sets, unlike a linear scan in a list.
  • No get(i) and no insertion order: traversal follows the hash table's own arrangement.
  • List vs Set: choose List when order and duplicates matter (marks, steps, history), Set when membership must be unique (IDs, hashtags).

jv4_14 adds a duplicate "java" and HashSet quietly refuses - then compares with an ArrayList that keeps both "tea" entries.

title.en: Types of errors: compile-time, runtime, logical

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
avg (wrong) = 16.0
logic bugs compile + run

expl.en:
The three species of program error:

  • Compile-time: grammar or type mistakes; javac refuses to build the .class file.
  • Runtime (an exception): compiles fine, crashes while running - divide by zero, null reference.
  • Logical: runs perfectly and prints the WRONG answer - the hardest kind, no one flags it for you.

The logical bug above: sum / 2 happens before + 1, so 16.0 prints where +10 was intended. Only careful testing catches such bugs.

title.en: Division by zero without try-catch (program crashes)

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
before the crash
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
	at Main.main(Main.java:7)

expl.en:
This is what an unhandled exception does: the program stops dead at the line marks / subjects.

  • The JVM creates an ArithmeticException object and looks for a handler - finds none.
  • So it prints the stack trace (Exception in thread "main", the exception name, and the exact line number) and terminates.
  • The last println never executes - proof that the crash killed the rest of main().

The next program catches exactly this politely, with try-catch.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
try: computing...
caught: / by zero
program continues...
avg = 90.0

expl.en:
Practical 13 (part 1). Put risky code in try, put recovery in catch:

  • As soon as the division throws, control jumps to the matching catch - e is the exception object.
  • e.getMessage() gives the detail: / by zero.
  • After catch finishes, normal flow resumes - the program ends gracefully instead of crashing.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
try to read length...
caught a null pointer!
name was never set
still running fine

expl.en:
Practical 13 (part 2). A reference holding null points to nothing - calling a method on it throws NullPointerException.

  • Fix it by catching, or better: check if (name != null) before touching it.
  • NPE is the most common exception in real Java code; careful design avoids returning null at all.

title.en: try-catch: stepping past the end of an array

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
marks[0] = 80
marks[1] = 75
marks[2] = 90
caught: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Index 3 out of bounds for length 3
loop recovered

expl.en:
Arrays know their own size; stepping outside 0 .. length-1 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

  • Here i <= 3 is the classic off-by-one slip - the report names it exactly (see the printed class name and message).
  • We caught the parent RuntimeException and asked the object its own type with getSimpleName() - proof that this exception is part of the runtime family.
  • Simply writing i < marks.length makes this exception impossible.

title.en: Multiple catch blocks: first match wins

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
small = 5
not a valid int value
done either way

expl.en:
One try may have several catch blocks; the JVM walks them top-down and runs the first whose type fits.

  • parseInt("99999999999") overflows int and throws NumberFormatException, so the first catch runs.
  • Only ONE catch block runs per exception.
  • Order matters: specific children first, general Exception last - a parent catch written first would swallow everything (and javac rejects unreachable catches).

title.en: finally: runs whether or not an exception occurs

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
open vault
pay out 500
close vault (always!)
---------
open vault
transaction failed
close vault (always!)

expl.en:
finally is the "whatever happens" block - it runs:

  • when the try completes normally (first call),
  • when an exception is caught (second call),
  • even when an exception is NOT caught (right before the crash).

That is why it is the correct place for cleanup: closing files, releasing locks, logging out. Notice how "close vault" prints in both runs of bank().

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
voter card approved
rejected:
age 15 is below 18
registration desk closed

expl.en:
throw lets your own code raise an exception object:

  • Syntax: throw new ExceptionType(message) - one single object, created on the spot.
  • The rest of the method is skipped; the nearest matching catch (here, in main) takes over.
  • Use it to reject impossible input - classic for validation rules like a minimum voting age.

Practical 13 shape: a built-in exception type raised deliberately, with our own message, handled by try-catch.

title.en: throws: declaring that a method may fail

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
sleeping 300ms...
awake!
sleeping 100ms...
awake!
end of a quiet day

expl.en:
throws belongs to a method's signature: it advertises "calling me might raise this checked exception - handle it or pass it on".

  • Thread.sleep() is declared throws InterruptedException, so every caller must catch it or re-declare throws.
  • Here we choose to declare it again on main() - the JVM tolerates that.
  • throw = actually raise; throws = merely warn in the header. They are NOT interchangeable.

title.en: throw + throws together in a real method

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
paid out 1500
ATM error:
not enough balance: 2000
thank you, visit again

expl.en:
The typical business-method pairing:

  • throws IllegalStateException in the header warns callers "this may fail";
  • throw new ... inside enforces the rule (amount must fit the balance);
  • The caller decides politely: catch the fault and show a human message instead of crashing the ATM screen.

IllegalStateException is unchecked; a checked exception would have FORCED the caller to handle it at compile time.

title.en: Catch order: subclass before the superclass

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
1st: specific - NPE
narrow ones first!

expl.en:
Catch blocks are matched top to bottom by type:

  • The thrown object is a NullPointerException, so the first catch prints - not the parent RuntimeException one below it.
  • Had we written catch (Exception e) first, the child catches would be unreachable and javac would complain.
  • Rule of thumb: go up the hierarchy as you go down the catch list - most specific first, most general last.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
team = [Meera, Zoya, Ravi, Farhan]
size = 4
after remove: [Zoya, Ravi]
has Zoya? true
Ravi at index 1
first = Zoya

expl.en:
Practical 14 (part A). ArrayList<String> is the growable array of the Collections framework - the diamond names the element type.

  • add() grows the list; the two-argument add inserts in the middle.
  • remove() works by value or by index; size() replaces array length.
  • Search trio: contains() answers yes/no, indexOf() answers where, get(i) fetches.
  • Printing the list shows [a, b, c] - ArrayList brings its own friendly toString.

title.en: ArrayList traversal: for-each loop in action

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
--- index loop ---
0: 82
1: 95
2: 67
3: 88
--- for-each loop ---
total = 332
average = 83.0

expl.en:
Practical 14 (part B). Two traversal styles:

  • The classic counting loop gives the index k - useful when position matters.
  • The for-each loop for (int m : marks) reads naturally ("for each mark m in marks") and can never walk past the end.
  • Autoboxing quietly wraps int into Integer on add and unwraps on use - you saw it in Unit 2; here the glove work pays off.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
tags = [exam, coding, java]
size = 3
has exam? true
after remove: [exam, java]
--- each unique tag ---
* exam
* java
list dup ok: [tea, tea]

expl.en:
Practical 14 (part C). HashSet = a bag that refuses duplicates:

  • Four adds, one repeated "java" - size() stays honest at 3.
  • contains() on a HashSet is a hash-table lookup: very fast even with thousands of members.
  • Traversal uses the same for-each loop as a list, but the order is not insertion order - it follows the hash table, so never rely on it.
  • Compare the ArrayList at the end: lists happily keep duplicates; sets do not. Use a set for unique tags/friends/roll numbers and a list when order and duplicates matter.

terms.en: risky code in try, recovery in catch
first matching catch runs; only one
throws warns callers, throw does it
unique members, no order, no index
visit every element, no index needed

q.en: Name the three types of errors in Java.

a.en: Compile-time (javac stops it), runtime (exception while running) and logical (runs but wrong answer).

q.en: Which error type is hardest to find and why?

a.en: Logical - nothing flags it; the program simply produces the wrong output, so only testing reveals it.

q.en: What is an exception?

a.en: An object the JVM creates at run time describing a failure - it carries the type (e.g. ArithmeticException), a message and the stack trace.

q.en: What happens to an uncaught exception?

a.en: The JVM prints the stack trace and terminates the program; statements after the throwing line never run.

q.en: What is the root class of all throwables?

a.en: Throwable - with two children: Error (serious, not caught) and Exception (application-level, catchable).

q.en: Checked vs unchecked exceptions?

a.en: Checked: javac forces try-catch or throws (InterruptedException, IOException). Unchecked: RuntimeException children - the compiler stays silent (ArithmeticException, NPE).

q.en: List five built-in unchecked exceptions.

a.en: ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, NumberFormatException, IllegalArgumentException.

q.en: What causes a NullPointerException?

a.en: Calling a method or touching a field through a reference that holds null (no object behind it).

q.en: What is the message of integer divide by zero?

a.en: The ArithmeticException carries "/ by zero".

q.en: What do try and catch do?

a.en: try wraps risky statements; catch (Type e) receives the thrown object and runs recovery - one catch handles one exception family.

q.en: Which statements are skipped when an exception is thrown?

a.en: The rest of the try block; control jumps straight to the matching catch.

q.en: What does e.getMessage() give?

a.en: The detail string of the exception - for division by zero, "/ by zero".

q.en: When does finally run?

a.en: Always: after normal try completion, after a caught exception, and even when nothing catches (right before the program dies).

q.en: Give two good uses of finally.

a.en: Closing files/connections and releasing locks - cleanup that must happen on every path.

q.en: Can finally exist without catch?

a.en: Yes - try-finally is legal; the exception still propagates after finally runs. Catching is simpler for beginners.

q.en: How many catch blocks can follow one try? How many run?

a.en: Any number may follow, but exactly one runs - the first whose type matches.

q.en: Which catch must come first: Exception or NullPointerException?

a.en: NullPointerException - specific children before parent types, otherwise the parent shadows them (javac error).

q.en: How does the JVM pick a catch block?

a.en: Top to bottom, first block whose declared type IS-A supertype of the thrown object.

q.en: What does throw do, and what follows it?

a.en: It raises an exception object immediately: throw new ArithmeticException("msg"); - a NEW object, so the keyword is followed by a constructor call.

q.en: Give a real use of throw.

a.en: Input validation - rejecting age below 18 or an overdrawn amount before corrupt data spreads.

q.en: What does throws declare?

a.en: That a method may raise the listed checked exceptions - a warning in the signature, not an action.

q.en: Difference between throw and throws?

a.en: throw is a statement in the body that raises one object; throws is a clause in the header listing possible checked exceptions.

q.en: If a method says throws InterruptedException, what must callers do?

a.en: Either wrap the call in try-catch or declare throws again in their own header.

q.en: Why is Thread.sleep() special for beginners?

a.en: It declares throws InterruptedException, so callers are FORCED to handle or declare - a convenient checked-exception example.

q.en: Is IllegalArgumentException checked or unchecked?

a.en: Unchecked (a RuntimeException child) - the compiler does not force handling; good design still catches it.

q.en: Practical 13: which two exceptions are demonstrated?

a.en: ArithmeticException (divide by zero) and NullPointerException - each caught with try-catch-finally.

q.en: Why do we need the Collections framework?

a.en: Arrays are fixed-size and low-level; programs need growable containers with add, remove and search built in - ArrayList, HashSet etc. of java.util.

q.en: Name the root interface and two child interfaces.

a.en: Collection; children List and Set (Queue too).

q.en: Which classes implement List and Set for this course?

a.en: ArrayList implements List; HashSet implements Set.

q.en: Can collections store primitive int directly?

a.en: No - only objects; autoboxing wraps int into Integer automatically when you add it.

q.en: What does the diamond <> do in ArrayList<String>?

a.en: Names the element type (generics); the compiler then rejects anything that is not a String.

q.en: How is add(i, e) different from add(e)?

a.en: add(e) appends at the end; add(i, e) inserts at index i, shifting the rest right.

q.en: Two ways to remove from an ArrayList?

a.en: By value - remove("Farhan"); or by index - remove(0).

q.en: Search trio of ArrayList?

a.en: contains(e) -> boolean, indexOf(e) -> position or -1, get(i) -> element.

q.en: How do you get the length-equivalent of an ArrayList?

a.en: size() - a method, unlike array's length field.

q.en: What prints when you println an ArrayList?

a.en: A friendly [a, b, c] form - ArrayList implements toString().

q.en: What is the for-each loop form?

a.en: for (Type x : collection) { ... } - visits every element in order, no counter needed.

q.en: Two limitations of for-each?

a.en: No index available inside, and you cannot add/remove elements of the same collection during the loop.

q.en: What does HashSet do with a duplicate add?

a.en: Silently ignores it - the set keeps one copy; size() does not grow.

q.en: How does a HashSet find members so fast?

a.en: Hashing: the element's hashCode points to its bucket, so contains() is near-instant instead of a full scan.

q.en: Does HashSet keep insertion order?

a.en: No - traversal follows the hash table's arrangement; never rely on the order.

q.en: ArrayList vs HashSet: duplicates and order?

a.en: ArrayList keeps duplicates in insertion order; HashSet forbids duplicates and promises no order.

q.en: When do you pick a Set over a List?

a.en: When membership must be unique - tags, roll numbers- and order does not matter.

q.en: Practical 14: which operations are shown on ArrayList and HashSet?

a.en: add, remove, search (contains/indexOf) and traversal with a for-each loop on both collections.

q.en: Which exception fires if a list is modified during for-each?

a.en: ConcurrentModificationException - the iterator notices the structure changed.
